raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old male patient had gradual short-term memory decline and word-finding difficulty for 2 years. However, his ambulation and instrumental activities of daily living were otherwise intact. He was ever admitted to our hospital because of systemic cryptococcosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia infection. At that time, CSF study revealed elevated total protein (92.9 mg/dL); glucose and the lymphocyte count were within normal limits. India ink and cryptococcal antigen staining of CSF were negative. Brain MRI showed numerous infarcts and microbleeds in the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres. During hospitalization, an acute change in consciousness to a comatose state occurred. Brain computed tomography (CT) revealed cerebellar hemorrhage with hydrocephalus. Therefore, the patient received suboccipital craniectomy and evacuation of the cerebellar hematoma. He recovered consciousness after surgery. He then resumed orientation and ambulation after amphotericin B treatment for systemic cryptococcosis and rehabilitation for 1 month. The patient was discharged with oral fluconazole and no events were observed during follow-up.
However, 2 months after the discharge, he came to our hospital again due to newly developed symptoms including forgetfulness, ideational apraxia, left hemineglect, personality changes, and agitation for 3 weeks. He was then admitted for further survey. The brain MRI showed bilateral cerebral hemispheres FLAIR hyperintensities (Figures 2A-C) and multiple cortical-subcortical microbleeds (Figure 2D). Moreover, superficial siderosis were seen in the surface of brain stem and cerebellum (not shown in figure), which was probably owing to previous surgery of cerebellar hematoma evacuation. CSF study showed elevated total protein, but no evidence of cryptococcal infection or bacterial meningoencephalitis. EEG showed mild to moderate diffuse cortical dysfunction with emphasis in the right frontocentral area. Due to the patient's previous history, central nervous system (CNS) cryptococcosis was suspected. Intravenous induction therapy with amphotericin B and mannitol were initiated in the beginning, but the clinical symptoms of cognitive deficits persisted.
Due to the suspicion of probable CAA-ri, intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) was administered for 2 weeks. The cognitive function of the patient improved 1 week after the initiation of steroid therapy. Oral prednisolone treatment with a tapering course was prescribed for 2 months after discharge. Follow-up EEG normalized. Brain MRI (Figures 2E-G) 4 months after discharge showed resolution of the edematous changes, but the number of cerebral microbleed increased (Figure 2H).
The patient received amyloid PET about 6 months after the resolution of the edematous changes on MRI. The amyloid PET showed diffuse amyloid deposition especially in the bilateral frontal and posterior temporal regions. The higher amyloid burden area did not significantly correlate with the previous area of FLAIR hyperintensities. No significant tau deposition was noted (Figure 2J). His APOE genotype was epsilon3/epsilon3. His clinical status remained stable during outpatient follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male presented with 3 weeks of newly developed forgetfulness, ideational apraxia, left hemineglect, personality changes, and agitation, on a background of 2 years of gradual short-term memory decline and word-finding difficulty.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a 2-year history of gradual short-term memory decline and word-finding difficulty with preserved ambulation and instrumental activities of daily living. He had previously been hospitalized for systemic cryptococcosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (during which CSF showed protein 92.9 mg/dL with negative India ink and CrAg, brain MRI showed bilateral infarcts and microbleeds, and he underwent suboccipital craniectomy and hematoma evacuation for acute cerebellar hemorrhage with hydrocephalus, recovering after 1 month of amphotericin B and rehabilitation and discharging on oral fluconazole). Two months after discharge, he developed 3 weeks of acute forgetfulness, ideational apraxia, left hemineglect, personality changes, and agitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior hospitalization 2 months earlier for systemic cryptococcosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia complicated by cerebellar hemorrhage with hydrocephalus status post suboccipital craniectomy and hematoma evacuation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for memory decline, word-finding difficulty, ideational apraxia, left hemineglect, personality changes, and agitation. Home medications included oral fluconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Exhibited forgetfulness, ideational apraxia, left hemineglect, personality changes, and agitation on readmission.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI on readmission showed bilateral cerebral hemispheric FLAIR hyperintensities, multiple cortical-subcortical microbleeds, and brainstem/cerebellar superficial siderosis. CSF analysis showed elevated total protein but no evidence of cryptococcal infection or bacterial meningoencephalitis. EEG showed mild-to-moderate diffuse cortical dysfunction emphasized in the right frontocentral area. Amyloid PET performed 6 months after MRI edema resolution demonstrated diffuse amyloid deposition in bilateral frontal and posterior temporal regions without significant tau deposition.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation (CAA-ri) following prior resolved systemic cryptococcosis, confirmed by characteristic MRI asymmetric confluent FLAIR hyperintensities with multiple cortical-subcortical microbleeds, diffuse amyloid deposition on amyloid PET, steroid responsiveness, and exclusion of CNS cryptococcal relapse or bacterial meningoencephalitis on CSF analysis. Initial empirical IV amphotericin B and mannitol for suspected CNS cryptococcosis failed to improve cognition; switching to IV methylprednisolone (40 mg/day for 2 weeks) resulted in cognitive improvement within 1 week, followed by a 2-month oral prednisolone taper. Follow-up EEG normalized, 4-month MRI showed resolution of edematous changes (with increased microbleeds), and the patient remained clinically stable on outpatient follow-up.
